papers.title: Theses by publication in Spain: output, authorship and integrity concerns
papers.abstract: Theses by publication are accepted in most Spanish universities, yet there is little empirical evidence on the scientific output that supports them or on the role doctoral candidates play in that output, and it is not even possible to determine what share of all theses defended in the country follow this format. To address this gap, we analysed a sample of 338 theses by publication defended in Spain in 2025 and 2026, identified in the Teseo database and downloaded in full text. On average, each thesis included 4.0 works, of which 3.0 were articles indexed in Scopus, and 61.1% of these articles appeared in first-quartile SJR journals. The doctoral candidate was first author in 81.1% of the articles and held an intermediate position in 12.1%, while 17 candidates (5.4%) were not first or sole author of any article in their compendium. As for publication venues, MDPI was the main publisher, with 23.2% of the articles, and 40.6% of the candidates published at least one work from their compendium with it. Overall, 45.4% of the candidates used so-called grey publishers, such as MDPI or Frontiers, at least once, and for almost 10% of them these publishers were the only outlet for the compendium. We also detected other infrequent but questionable practices, such as the inclusion of works published in journals delisted from Scopus or in special issues guest-edited by the candidates themselves, works still under review, and articles included in two different theses. Taken together, these results point to the need to clarify regulations on theses by publication, in particular regarding the candidate's authorship of the works linked to the thesis and the quality criteria required of publication venues. Theses by publication should also be identified in a standardised way in official registers, so that they can be retrieved and monitored.

papers.title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
papers.abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.

papers.title: Embedding or bridging? AI4Science teams differ more in knowledge recombination than in problem novelty
papers.abstract: AI for Science (AI4Science) is reshaping scientific research, yet how the organization of AI-related and domain-scientific work relates to different dimensions of research performance remains poorly understood. We analyze 489,409 AI4Science articles published between 1990 and 2025, identifying seven affiliation-based organizational configurations comprising three forms of embedding and four forms of cross-unit bridging. Focusing on 2006-2025, we examine two dimensions of research performance: knowledge creation, characterized by scientific problem novelty and knowledge-recombination breadth, and research impact, assessed through journal placement and citation impact. We find that organizational configurations differ only modestly in problem novelty but substantially in knowledge-recombination breadth. Cross-unit bridging is consistently associated with broader knowledge recombination, particularly in AI-oriented bridging, without a corresponding advantage in problem novelty. However, greater recombination breadth does not necessarily align with stronger research impact. Science-oriented and Multi-orientation bridging exhibit the most consistent positive associations with JCI Q1 journal placement and citation impact, although neither shows a statistically significant adjusted advantage in publication in the Elite-4 journals (Nature, Science, Cell, and PNAS). These research-impact differences remain largely intact after accounting for problem novelty and recombination breadth. Our findings reveal that organizational configurations are associated with distinct patterns of knowledge creation and research impact, rather than a single hierarchy of research performance. The results highlight the importance of considering organizational arrangements in relation to specific scientific objectives, rather than assuming that any one configuration is universally superior.
